question: Explain the difference between an array and a linked list. When would you use each?
keyConcepts: arrays store elements in contiguous memory
linked lists connect nodes using pointers|references
arrays give fast bigo1|constant index|indexed|random access
linked lists insert|insertion|delete|deletion easily without shifting|moving elements

contradictions.note: Linked lists do not give O(1) random access; you must traverse from the head, which is O(n).
Linked lists do not give O(1) random access; you must traverse from the head, which is O(n).
Arrays give O(1) access by index, not O(n).

sampleIdealAnswer: An array stores elements in contiguous memory, so it gives O(1) random access by index, but inserting or deleting in the middle needs shifting elements and its size is usually fixed. A linked list stores nodes connected by pointers, so insertion and deletion are cheap once you have the node, but reaching an element needs O(n) traversal. Use an array for fast lookups and a linked list for frequent insertions and deletions.

question: What is the difference between a stack and a queue? Give a real use for each.
keyConcepts: stack is lifo last in first out
push and pop happen at the top|same|one end
queue is fifo first in first out
enqueue at the rear and dequeue from the front

contradictions.note: A stack is LIFO (last in, first out); a queue is FIFO.
A queue is FIFO (first in, first out); a stack is LIFO.

sampleIdealAnswer: A stack is LIFO: the last element pushed is the first popped, and both operations happen at the top, like undo history or the call stack. A queue is FIFO: elements are enqueued at the rear and dequeued from the front, like a ticket line or a print queue. Both support these operations in O(1).

question: What is the difference between state and props in React, and when would you lift state up?
keyConcepts: props are read only inputs passed from a parent component
state is data owned and updated by the component itself
changing state triggers a rerender|render
lift state up to the nearest common parent when sibling components share data
sampleIdealAnswer: Props are read-only inputs a parent passes to a child component, while state is data a component owns and updates itself with something like useState. Changing state triggers a re-render. When two sibling components need the same data, I lift the state up to their nearest common parent and pass it down as props with callbacks.

question: Explain how REST APIs work and the difference between PUT and PATCH.
keyConcepts: rest models resources identified by urls and uses http methods
rest is stateless each request has all information
put replaces the entire resource
patch updates only part of a resource

contradictions.note: PATCH updates only part of a resource; PUT replaces the entire resource.

sampleIdealAnswer: REST models data as resources identified by URLs and uses HTTP methods such as GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE. It is stateless, so every request carries all the information the server needs, and status codes report the result. PUT replaces the entire resource and is idempotent, while PATCH updates only part of it.

question: Explain the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN with an example.
keyConcepts: inner join returns only rows that match in both tables
left join returns all rows from the left table
unmatched rows from the right table get null values
example such as customers and orders

contradictions.note: INNER JOIN returns only matching rows; LEFT JOIN keeps all rows of the left table.

sampleIdealAnswer: An INNER JOIN returns only the rows that have a match in both tables. A LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table and the matching rows from the right; where there is no match, the right-side columns are NULL. For example, joining customers with orders, an inner join lists only customers who ordered, while a left join also lists customers with no orders.

question: Walk me through what happens from the moment a user clicks Submit on a form to the data being saved.
keyConcepts: the client validates the input and sends an http request
the server validates again and processes the request
the data is written to the database
the server sends a response and the ui shows success or errors
sampleIdealAnswer: The browser first validates the fields, then sends an HTTP POST request to an API endpoint. The server routes it, validates the data again, applies business rules and writes the record to the database. It then returns a response, and the frontend updates the UI with a success message or shows errors if anything failed.

question: What is the difference between unit, integration and end-to-end testing?
keyConcepts: unit tests check small isolated pieces like a function
integration tests check that modules work together
end to end tests simulate a real user flow through the whole system
unit tests are fast and cheap while end to end tests are slower and costlier
sampleIdealAnswer: Unit tests check one small piece, such as a function, in isolation and run fast. Integration tests check that several modules, like the API and the database, work together. End-to-end tests simulate a real user flow through the whole application, so they give the most confidence but are slower and more expensive to maintain.

question: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
keyConcepts: a process is a running program with its own memory address space
threads inside a process share the same memory and resources
threads are lightweight and switch faster than processes
processes are isolated from each other while threads can affect each other
sampleIdealAnswer: A process is a running program with its own address space and resources. Threads live inside a process and share its memory and resources, which makes them lightweight and faster to create and context-switch. Processes are isolated from each other, whereas a bug in one thread can affect the others in the same process.

question: Explain how a hash table works and how collisions are handled.
keyConcepts: a hash function maps a key to a bucket index
lookups take bigo1 average time
collisions happen when two keys map to the same bucket
collisions are handled by chaining or open addressing probing
sampleIdealAnswer: A hash table uses a hash function to map each key to a bucket index, which gives O(1) average time for insert and lookup. A collision happens when two keys map to the same bucket; it is handled by chaining, where each bucket holds a linked list, or by open addressing with probing. Resizing keeps the load factor low so operations stay fast.

question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING in SQL?
keyConcepts: where filters individual rows before grouping
having filters groups after aggregation
having can use aggregate functions like count or sum
where cannot use aggregate functions
sampleIdealAnswer: WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping happens, so it cannot use aggregate functions. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and aggregation, so it can use COUNT, SUM or AVG. For example, I use WHERE to pick rows from 2024 and HAVING to keep only departments with more than ten employees.

question: What is the difference between var, let and const in JavaScript?
keyConcepts: var is function scoped and hoisted
let is block scoped and can be reassigned
const is block scoped and cannot be reassigned
const objects can still be mutated
sampleIdealAnswer: var is function-scoped and hoisted with an undefined value, so it can cause surprising bugs. let is block-scoped and can be reassigned, and const is block-scoped and cannot be reassigned, although an object or array declared with const can still be mutated. I use const by default and let when I need to reassign.

sampleIdealAnswer: A good bug report has a clear title, exact steps to reproduce, the expected result and the actual result, the environment such as browser and version, and the severity. I attach screenshots or logs as evidence and keep it concise so a developer can reproduce it without asking questions.

question: How would you handle missing values in a dataset?

sampleIdealAnswer: First I investigate how many values are missing and why. If few rows are affected I may drop them; otherwise I impute with the mean, median or mode depending on the distribution, or use interpolation for time series. I then check that the method does not distort the data or introduce bias, and sometimes add a flag column.
